clarifications.text: The slide credits him with the first microscope. Earlier microscopes existed; his important contribution was making effective instruments and observing microorganisms.
The slide spells his first name Mattias; the conventional spelling is Matthias.

The slide calls cyanobacteria unicellular algae and explains kary as genes. Cyanobacteria are photosynthetic bacteria, and the root refers to nucleus. Not all cyanobacteria occur as isolated single cells.

The microtubule description concerns eukaryotic cilia and flagella. Bacterial flagella have a different structure.
The slide groups all algae with cellulose-walled plants. Algal coverings vary; cellulose is common in some algal groups but is not a universal algal-wall rule.

The slide says ER is continuous with the cell membrane. ER is continuous with the outer nuclear envelope; transfer toward the Golgi and plasma membrane occurs through membrane traffic, rather than one uninterrupted ER-to-cell-surface membrane.
The source mentions strands of rRNA but leaves out ribosomal proteins. Both are components of a ribosome.
The slide associates polysomes with proteins needed within the cell. Polysomes are not limited to that destination; free or ER-associated ribosomes may form them.
The slide says Golgi may connect to ER. Teach the transport-vesicle connection rather than a general claim of direct, continuous membrane between the two organelles.

The slide calls the stacks thylakoids and puts all photosynthesis enzymes there. Distinguish individual thylakoids, grana stacks, and stroma; not all photosynthetic reactions occur in the thylakoid membrane.
Cholesterol is prominent in animal plasma-membrane models; do not assume every membrane in every organism has the same lipid composition.

The slide says small molecules pass freely. This is too broad: charge, polarity, and lipid solubility matter. The page 34 picture also wrongly depicts Cl- moving by simple diffusion through the lipid bilayer; ions need transport proteins.
High-to-low describes net movement, not a rule that every individual molecule moves in only one direction.
The source names channels only, but facilitated diffusion includes carriers. Its Cl- diagram must not be used as evidence that a charged ion freely crosses the lipid bilayer.
The slide says neutral molecules freely cross membranes. Neutrality alone is insufficient: large polar molecules can still face a barrier. Size, polarity, charge, and the pathway all matter.

The source says water moves in an attempt to equilibrate. Water has no intention; random motion and differences in water potential produce net movement. The simple solute comparison assumes similar pressures and a nonpenetrating solute.

Interpret concentration as effective nonpenetrating-solute concentration. Isotonic does not mean water molecules stop. Plant cell walls constrain swelling, so plant and animal cells need not show identical shape changes.

ATP directly powers primary active transport. Secondary active transport uses stored gradient energy indirectly supplied by metabolism. Large cargo generally uses vesicular transport rather than crossing through a pump as an intact large package.

The slide calls organelle membranes identical to the plasma membrane and mentions cholesterol everywhere. Membranes share a general bilayer plan but differ in proteins and lipids. Its ER-to-Golgi carrier is better described as a transport vesicle than a large vacuole.
The source ends with divide or die. Treat this as a simplified illustration of growth limits, not a universal outcome: cells can stop growing or use shapes and structures that improve exchange.
